formation.title: The Tang Restoration
formation.text:
Chang'an blazes with new glory. The ancient capital of the Tang, where once two million souls from every corner of the known world gathered beneath crimson palace gates, lives again. From Jingzhao to Kashgar, from the Yellow River to the Tianshan, an empire that once defined civilization itself stirs from centuries of slumber.

The Tang at its zenith was not merely a Chinese dynasty. It was a cosmopolitan world-empire where Turkic generals led Chinese armies, Persian merchants thronged the Western Market, and Buddhist sutras sat alongside Nestorian gospels and Manichaean hymns. Now the question falls to you: what shall define this restoration?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: March west! Restore the Protectorates beyond the Jade Gate.

modifiers.name: Restore the Protectorates
modifiers.text: The glory of Tang lies in its reach beyond the mountains. From the Jade Gate to the shores of the Caspian, the Protectorates General secured an empire spanning steppe, desert, and oasis. Through military might and diplomatic cunning, the Tang brought order to the Western Regions and controlled the arteries of continental trade.

options.text: Let the Brush conquer what the Sword cannot.

modifiers.name: Golden Age of Letters
modifiers.text: Under Tang patronage, every faith found welcome in Chang'an. Li Bai raised his cup to the moon, Du Fu mourned the suffering of the common people, and Wang Wei painted landscapes that dissolved the boundary between poetry and painting. Buddhist monks from India, Nestorian priests from Persia, and Manichaean missionaries from Central Asia debated freely in the shadow of the Daming Palace.

advances.name: Fubing Militia System
advances.text: The fubing system assigns land to farmer-soldiers who serve in rotation at the capital or frontier garrisons, providing a vast reserve of trained militia at minimal cost to the state.

advances.name: Equal-Field System
advances.text: The juntian system distributes state land equally among adult males, ensuring tax revenue while preventing dangerous concentrations of wealth in aristocratic hands.

advances.name: Imperial Post Roads
advances.text: A network of relay stations spaced every thirty li connects the capital to the furthest frontier provinces, enabling rapid communication, troop movement, and administrative control.

advances.name: Modao Heavy Infantry
advances.text: The modao, a devastating two-handed long blade, allows elite infantry to form impenetrable walls of steel against cavalry charges, a tradition born on Tang frontiers.

event.title: The Modao Infantry
event.text:
The modao, a fearsome two-handed sword nearly seven feet in length, was the signature weapon of Tang heavy infantry. Wielded in dense formations by select troops, the modao created a wall of steel that could stop a cavalry charge dead. At the Battle of the Mohe River in 732, the modao infantry of the Tang general Zhang Shougui broke wave after wave of Khitan cavalry, leaving the steppe warriors stunned by the discipline and killing power of these foot soldiers.

The modao required years of training and exceptional strength. Units equipped with these weapons were drawn from the most experienced soldiers of the frontier garrisons, men who had spent their lives fighting nomadic raiders and understood how to use terrain and formation to neutralize the mobility advantage of mounted enemies.

options.text: The modao speaks louder than any argument.

advances.name: Jiedushi Military Governorships
advances.text: Regional military commissioners exercise combined civil and military authority over frontier circuits, maintaining professional garrison armies to defend against nomadic incursions.

advances.name: Buddhist State Patronage
advances.text: Imperial sponsorship of Buddhist monasteries, translation projects, and pilgrim networks creates a vast religious infrastructure that enhances literacy, cultural exchange, and social stability.

advances.name: Xuanjia Heavy Cavalry
advances.text: The xuanjia, 'black armor' cataphracts, represent Tang heavy cavalry at its finest: fully armored riders on barded horses, capable of delivering devastating shock charges.

advances.name: Silk Road Mastery
advances.text: Tang control of the major Silk Road arteries transforms overland trade from a dangerous gamble into a regulated, profitable, and secure enterprise connecting East and West.

advances.name: Sancai Ceramic Tradition
advances.text: The distinctive three-color glazed pottery of the Tang (featuring amber, green, and cream tones) becomes both a cultural icon and a valuable export commodity.

advances.name: Nestorian Stele
advances.text: The erection of the Nestorian Stele in Chang'an symbolizes Tang religious pluralism, where Christianity, Islam, Manichaeism, Zoroastrianism, Buddhism, and Daoism coexist under imperial protection.

event.title: The Nestorian Stele
event.text:
In 781, a limestone stele was erected in Chang'an recording the arrival of Nestorian Christianity in China a century and a half earlier. The inscription, written in both Chinese and Syriac, tells how the Persian monk Aluoben arrived at the Tang court in 635 and was received by Emperor Taizong, who examined his scriptures and declared: 'The Way has no unchanging name, sages have no unchanging method. Teaching is established to suit the land, and secretly help all living things.'

This spirit of religious tolerance defined the Tang cosmopolis. Buddhist monasteries, Daoist temples, Zoroastrian fire altars, Manichaean light-houses, Islamic mosques, and Nestorian churches stood within the same city walls, each contributing to a civilization that measured greatness not by uniformity but by the breadth of its embrace.

options.text: All paths lead to truth under Tang heaven.

advances.name: Hanlin Academy
advances.text: The Hanlin Academy gathers the most brilliant scholars in the empire to draft imperial edicts, compose state documents, and advise on policy, a reservoir of administrative excellence.

advances.name: Frontier Horse Archers
advances.text: Recruited from the mixed populations of the frontier (Turkic, Sogdian, and Chinese) these fast-moving mounted archers serve as scouts, raiders, and flanking forces.

advances.name: Grotto Temple Devotion
advances.text: The great cave temple complexes at Dunhuang, Longmen, and Yungang represent centuries of devotional carving, painting, and sculpture, repositories of Buddhist art and scholarship.

advances.name: Anxi Protectorate
advances.text: The Protectorate General to Pacify the West controls the Tarim Basin through four garrisons at Kucha, Khotan, Kashgar, and Karashahr, securing the western approaches to the empire.

event.title: The Anxi Protectorate Restored
event.text:
In the year 640, Emperor Taizong established the Protectorate General to Pacify the West at Xizhou, later moving its seat to Kucha. At its height, the Anxi Protectorate commanded four major garrisons (at Kucha, Khotan, Kashgar, and Karashahr) securing the entire Tarim Basin and projecting Tang authority deep into Transoxiana.

The An Lushan Rebellion of 755 forced the withdrawal of Anxi's garrisons to defend the heartland, and the Protectorate was gradually lost to the Tibetan Empire and Turkic powers. Now, with our banners flying once more over the Western Regions, the Anxi Protectorate is restored, its relay stations, garrison towns, and caravan guards ensuring safe passage for merchants, monks, and diplomats alike.

options.text: The Western Regions are secure once more.

modifiers.name: Protectorate Restored
modifiers.text: The Protectorate General to Pacify the West has been reestablished, extending military authority across the Tarim Basin and the Tianshan passes. Garrisons secure the trade routes while mobile cavalry forces project power deep into the steppe.

options.text: A triumph, but the work continues.

advances.name: Imperial Silk Production
advances.text: State-controlled silk workshops produce the finest textiles in the world, from brocades woven with gold thread to gossamer-thin gauzes prized from Japan to Byzantium.

advances.name: Poetry Golden Age
advances.text: The Tang produces over 48,000 surviving poems by more than 2,200 authors. Li Bai, Du Fu, Wang Wei, and Bai Juyi establish the literary canon that will define Chinese civilization.

advances.name: Jinshi Examination Perfected
advances.text: The jinshi degree (testing literary composition, policy analysis, and moral philosophy) becomes the supreme pathway to government service, breaking aristocratic monopolies on power.

event.title: The Imperial Examination Perfected
event.text:
The keju examination, first systematized under the Sui, reached its golden form under the Tang. The jinshi degree, Presented Scholar, became the highest achievement a man could aspire to, tested not merely in rote memorization but in literary composition, policy analysis, and moral philosophy.

Under Empress Wu Zetian, the system was thrown open wider than ever before, breaking the grip of aristocratic families on government positions. The examination halls of Chang'an saw candidates from every province compete on merit alone. This meritocratic revolution produced statesmen like Zhang Jiuling, whose governance earned him the title of model chancellor for all dynasties to follow.

options.text: Let merit alone determine who serves the throne.

modifiers.name: Examination Perfected
modifiers.text: The jinshi examination system has been refined to its highest form. Any man of talent, regardless of birth, may rise to serve the Son of Heaven through literary excellence and administrative skill.

options.text: The examination is a tool, not a religion.

advances.name: Shencea Imperial Guards
advances.text: The Shencea Army, originally the Emperor's bodyguard, grows into the most powerful military force of the late Tang, numbering 150,000 professional soldiers.

advances.name: Sogdian Merchant Networks
advances.text: Sogdian merchants from Samarkand and Bukhara operate vast trading networks stretching from Chang'an to Constantinople, serving as the commercial backbone of the Silk Road.

advances.name: Tea-Horse Trade
advances.text: The strategic exchange of Chinese tea for nomadic horses creates a mutually dependent border economy that stabilizes frontier relations and provides the empire with superior cavalry mounts.

advances.name: Confessional Tolerance
advances.text: The Tang tradition of religious pluralism is extended and formalized, ensuring that communities of every faith contribute peacefully to the prosperity of the empire.

advances.name: Silk Road Renaissance
advances.text: A renewed wave of Silk Road commerce brings unprecedented wealth and cultural exchange, as improved infrastructure and diplomatic relationships open new trade corridors.

event.title: The Silk Road Renaissance
event.text:
The Silk Road under Tang management was not merely a trade route. It was the nervous system of Eurasian civilization. From Chang'an's bustling Western Market, caravans departed carrying silk, porcelain, tea, and paper westward through the Hexi Corridor and the Jade Gate, crossing the Taklamakan's northern and southern rim roads to reach Kashgar, Samarkand, Baghdad, and ultimately Constantinople.

In return came Arabian horses, Persian glass, Indian spices, Roman gold coins, and Central Asian music that transformed Tang court entertainment. Sogdian merchants, the 'FedEx of the ancient world', ran networks of trading houses from Chang'an to the Mediterranean. The Tang government maintained relay stations, regulated merchants, and garrisoned oasis towns, creating the safest and most profitable trade corridor the world had ever known.

options.text: The Road connects all peoples under heaven.

advances.name: Frontier Military Reform
advances.text: The frontier army is modernized with standardized equipment, professional training, and reformed command structures, creating a mobile and disciplined force.

advances.name: Grand Canal Integration
advances.text: The Grand Canal links the Yangtze rice surplus to the northern heartland, enabling massive internal trade and supporting the population of the capital region.

advances.name: Imperial Consolidation
advances.text: Imperial authority is extended and solidified through administrative reform, cultural integration, and the suppression of regional separatism.

advances.name: Woodblock Printing
advances.text:
Woodblock printing enables the mass reproduction of texts (Buddhist sutras, Confucian classics, and government decrees) spreading literacy and institutional knowledge across the empire.

Unlocks: Woodblock Print Shop

advances.name: Gunpowder Alchemy
advances.text: Tang alchemists seeking the elixir of immortality stumble upon a more immediate discovery: gunpowder. Fire arrows, incendiary bombs, and proto-rockets transform siege warfare.

advances.name: Centralized Bureaucracy
advances.text: The examination-based bureaucratic system reaches full maturity, producing a governing class selected entirely on merit and loyalty to the central court.

advances.name: Maritime Silk Road
advances.text: As overland routes face disruption, maritime trade through Guangzhou, Quanzhou, and the South China Sea grows to rival and eventually exceed the continental Silk Road in volume.

advances.name: Porcelain Export Mastery
advances.text:
Chinese porcelain, 'white gold', becomes the most sought-after commodity in world trade. Ship after ship carries blue-and-white wares to markets from Zanzibar to Lisbon.

Available in: Sancai Ceramic Kiln

advances.name: Standing Frontier Army
advances.text: The frontier garrison system evolves into a permanent standing army, with professional soldiers serving year-round in well-supplied fortified positions along the border.

advances.name: Cosmopolitan Court
advances.text: The imperial court welcomes talent from every nation and culture, integrating foreign administrators, generals, artists, and merchants into the fabric of governance.

advances.name: Formalized Tea Culture
advances.text: Lu Yu's Classic of Tea established the philosophy and practice of tea preparation as high art. Tea houses become centers of social life, diplomacy, and literary exchange.

advances.name: Strategic Border Management
advances.text: A comprehensive system of walls, passes, garrison towns, and diplomatic protocols creates a layered defense-in-depth along the northern and western frontiers.

advances.name: Industrial Silk Production
advances.text: Mechanized looms and organized factory production transform silk manufacture from artisanal craft to industrial enterprise, and sericulture stations send clean silkworm eggs to the growers, vastly increasing output and export capacity.

advances.name: Modern Academy System
advances.text: The traditional examination system evolves to incorporate modern subjects (science, engineering, foreign languages) while retaining its meritocratic foundations.

advances.name: Continental Rail Network
advances.text: Iron rails trace the ancient Silk Road corridors, connecting Chang'an to the western frontier and beyond with speed and reliability the camel caravans could never match.

advances.name: Modern Army Reform
advances.text: The frontier garrison tradition is transformed into a modern professional army with standardized training, equipment, and tactical doctrine drawn from global military science.

advances.name: Cultural Renaissance
advances.text: A new generation of artists, poets, and thinkers draws on the Tang literary canon to create a cultural renaissance that celebrates both heritage and innovation.

advances.name: Silk Road Revival
advances.text: Modern infrastructure, diplomatic agreements, and commercial treaties revive the ancient Silk Road as a thriving corridor of trade, connecting East Asian markets to Central Asia and beyond.

destiny.name: Destiny of the Tang
destiny.text: The Tang Dynasty has been restored. With stability secured, the Son of Heaven must now choose a path for the empire's future: westward conquest to reclaim the Protectorates, or inward cultivation of the arts and learning that defined Tang civilization at its peak.

event.title: The Mandate Endures
event.text:
The empire stands stable. From the terraces of the Daming Palace, the restored Tang surveys a realm at peace, a realm that awaits the direction its new master will give it. The question before the Son of Heaven is not whether the Tang will endure, but what form its endurance will take.

The ancestors built an empire that straddled the known world. They also built a civilization that illuminated it. Both paths lie open.

options.text: The mandate endures.

destiny.name: Silk Road Command
destiny.text: Secure the great Silk Road cities of Samarkand and Bukhara. Control of these ancient crossroads means dominion over the richest trade arteries connecting East and West.

conditions.text: Own Samarkand, or a subject owns it
Own Bukhara, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Four Garrisons Secured
event.text:
When General Guo Xiaoke captured Kucha in 648, he established the pattern for all Tang operations in the Western Regions: swift cavalry strikes followed by permanent garrison towns connected by relay stations. Now Samarkand and Bukhara, cities that even Emperor Taizong only reached through diplomacy, fly our banner.

Sogdian merchants who once traded under Turkic protection now acknowledge Tang suzerainty. The great bazaars of Transoxiana funnel their wealth eastward along roads patrolled by our cavalry. What Taizong dreamed: we have accomplished.

options.text: The Silk Road answers to the Dragon Throne.

destiny.name: Steppe Hegemony
destiny.text: Extend Tang authority over the Mongol heartland at Karakorum and the Bactrian gateway at Balkh. The steppe must bow to the Dragon Throne before the march can continue.

conditions.text: Own Karakorum, or a subject owns it
Own Balkh, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Steppe Bows
event.text:
Karakorum, seat of Genghis Khan's empire, now acknowledges Tang authority. Balkh, the 'Mother of Cities' that Alexander the Great once conquered, falls under our protection. The steppe peoples who for centuries threatened the northern frontier have been brought within the imperial order.

This achievement surpasses anything the original Tang accomplished. Even at its zenith, the Tang's control of the steppe was contested and temporary. We have made it permanent. The question now is how best to govern these vast conquests.

options.text: Extract tribute to fund imperial expansion.

modifiers.name: Iron Tribute
modifiers.text: Conquered steppe peoples pay tribute in horses, livestock, and silver, enriching the imperial treasury and funding further campaigns of expansion.

options.text: Adopt nomadic mobility for our armies.

modifiers.name: Steppe Logistics
modifiers.text: Nomadic riding techniques and the vast horse herds of the conquered steppe peoples have been integrated into Tang military doctrine, enhancing army speed and recovery.

destiny.name: Tianxia Restored
destiny.text: Complete the restoration of All Under Heaven by planting Tang banners in Delhi and Baghdad. These two ancient capitals mark the furthest horizon of Tang ambition, a universal empire stretching from the Yellow River to the Euphrates.

conditions.text: Own Delhi, or a subject owns it
Own Baghdad, or a subject owns it

event.title: All Under Heaven
event.text:
Delhi and Baghdad, twin poles of world civilization, now acknowledge the supremacy of the Dragon Throne. No empire in history has achieved what we have accomplished: a single sovereign authority stretching from the rice paddies of the Yangtze to the bazaars of Mesopotamia, from the steppes of Mongolia to the Gangetic plain.

The Tang at its original height was one great power among several. The Tang restored is something else entirely, a universal empire that has absorbed or subordinated every major civilization on the Eurasian mainland. The concept of Tianxia, 'All Under Heaven,' is no longer a philosophical ideal. It is a geopolitical reality.

options.text: Establish the Pax Sinica across all lands.

modifiers.name: Pax Sinica
modifiers.text: With all major civilizations under Tang authority, a universal peace descends. The roads are safe, and peoples of every origin settle within the cosmopolitan Tang order.

options.text: The mandate demands eternal expansion.

modifiers.name: Mandate of Conquest
modifiers.text: The Son of Heaven's mandate demands that all lands acknowledge his sovereignty. Each new victory amplifies Tang prestige and reduces the cost of further campaigns.

destiny.name: The Literary Canon
destiny.text: Cultivate a literary and institutional renaissance that surpasses even the original Tang golden age. Gather the canon in a library at Chang'an, the city of the poets, and raise the city above what it was.

conditions.text: Owns Chang'an (Jingzhao) and it has a Library
Owns Chang'an (Jingzhao) and its development is at least 43

event.title: The New Literary Canon
event.text:
Li Bai wrote of moonlight and wine. Du Fu mourned the suffering of the common people. Wang Wei painted landscapes that dissolved the boundary between word and image. For centuries, their works defined the summit of human literary achievement.

Now a new generation of poets, essayists, and philosophers has emerged, heirs to the Tang tradition who have absorbed and transcended it. The library of Chang'an funds scholarly expeditions. Its copyists spread knowledge faster than ever before. The empire's vast population, more literate than ever, hungers for texts of every kind.

options.text: A new golden age of letters begins.

destiny.name: Universal Learning
destiny.text: Make the Tang capital the center of world commerce and scholarship. Ensure silk flows through your markets and fill your treasury to fund the greatest academy system the world has ever seen.

children.text: Silk is produced in the market
Silk is traded in the market

event.title: The Academy of All Nations
event.text:
The original Hanlin Academy gathered China's finest minds in a single institution. What we have built dwarfs it in every dimension. Our academies attract scholars from every nation, Persian astronomers, Indian mathematicians, Turkic linguists, Korean historians. Silk revenue funds endowed chairs and research programs.

The capital's markets overflow with the products of this intellectual ferment: astronomical instruments, medical treatises, geographical atlases, and engineering manuals. Where Tang scholars once translated Buddhist sutras from Sanskrit, our academics synthesize knowledge from every tradition into a unified corpus.

options.text: Found academies across the empire.

modifiers.name: Academy Network
modifiers.text: A network of imperial academies across the provinces raises literacy and food production through the application of scholarly knowledge to agriculture and governance.

options.text: Let merchants and scholars enrich each other.

modifiers.name: Merchant Scholars
modifiers.text: The fusion of commercial wealth and scholarly ambition produces a class of merchant-scholars who extend Tang cultural influence through trade routes reaching every corner of the known world.

destiny.name: The Celestial Mandate
destiny.text: Achieve the ultimate synthesis of knowledge and civilization. Rebuild Luoyang, the eastern capital, to twice its size, give it a library or a woodblock print shop for its books, and demonstrate that Tang learning encompasses all fields of human inquiry.

conditions.text: Owns Luoyang and it has a Library or a Woodblock Print Shop
Owns Luoyang and its development is at least 76

event.title: The Celestial Library
event.text:
The Siku Quanshu, the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, was a dream of total knowledge: every book worth preserving, copied, catalogued, and stored for eternity. We have surpassed even that ambition.

Our Imperial Library contains not merely Chinese texts but the accumulated wisdom of every civilization our scholars have encountered. Greek philosophy sits beside Buddhist metaphysics. Arab algebra illuminates Confucian cosmology. Indian medicine complements Chinese pharmacology. This is not merely a collection of books. It is the complete intellectual heritage of humanity, gathered under one roof and synthesized into a coherent whole.

options.text: Harmony of all learning under heaven.

modifiers.name: Confucian Synthesis
modifiers.text: A grand synthesis of Confucian, Buddhist, and Daoist thought produces a unified philosophical framework that reduces the cost of institutional adoption and strengthens administrative control.

options.text: Let a hundred schools of thought contend.

modifiers.name: Hundred Schools Reborn
modifiers.text: Intellectual pluralism flourishes as competing schools of thought (Legalist, Mohist, Daoist, Confucian, and foreign traditions) drive innovation in every field of human knowledge.

units.name: Modao Infantry
units.text: Elite heavy infantry wielding the fearsome modao, a seven-foot two-handed blade capable of cutting through horse and rider alike. These anti-cavalry specialists form impenetrable walls of steel.

units.name: Xuanjia Heavy Cavalry
units.text: The 'Black Armor' cataphracts of the Tang, fully armored riders on barded horses, delivering devastating shock charges that shatter enemy formations.

units.name: Frontier Horse Archers
units.text: Light cavalry recruited from the frontier's mixed populations, Turkic, Sogdian, and Chinese. Fast, agile raiders expert at scouting, flanking, and harassing enemy supply lines.

units.name: Shencea Imperial Guards
units.text: The elite Shencea Army, originally the Emperor's personal bodyguard, evolved into the most powerful military formation of the late Tang, professional, disciplined, and fiercely loyal.

units.name: Fubing Militia
units.text: Farmer-soldiers serving in rotation under the fubing system, providing a vast reserve of trained infantry at minimal cost to the state.

units.name: Frontier Levy Cavalry
units.text: Mixed Turkic and Chinese steppe riders raised from the frontier garrisons, combining nomadic riding skill with Tang military discipline.

buildings.name: Silk Road Caravanserai
buildings.text: A fortified waystation along the Silk Road providing shelter, food, fodder, and a secure marketplace for merchant caravans traversing the western trade routes.

buildings.name: Sancai Ceramic Kiln
buildings.text: Specialized kilns producing the famous Tang sancai (tri-color glazed pottery in amber, green, and cream) prized as luxury goods and diplomatic gifts across Eurasia.

buildings.name: Frontier Garrison
buildings.text: A jiedushi military command post on the frontier, maintaining a permanent professional garrison to defend against nomadic incursions and project imperial authority.

buildings.name: Buddhist Grotto Temple
buildings.text: A cave temple complex carved into cliffsides, decorated with painted murals and carved Buddhas. Centers of devotion, scholarship, and artistic achievement in the Tang Buddhist tradition.

buildings.name: Hanlin Imperial Academy
buildings.text: The highest scholarly institution of the empire, where the most brilliant jinshi graduates draft imperial edicts, compile histories, and advise the Son of Heaven on matters of state.

buildings.name: Woodblock Print Shop
buildings.text: A workshop of block carvers and printers. Texts are cut in reverse into pear and jujube wood, inked and pressed onto paper, sheet after sheet.

buildings.name: Imperial Silk Workshop
buildings.text: An imperial weaving office in a silk town, supervised by the state and paid in the silk levy. Its looms make brocades, gauzes and damasks for the court, and its demand keeps every mulberry grower of the district at work, so the town's own silk harvest is larger for it.

where.text: The location's raw material is Silk

buildings.name: Sericulture Station
buildings.text: A station on silk land where the moths are checked under the microscope and only clean eggs, laid on paper cards, go out to the growers. Silkworm disease no longer empties the rearing houses, and the cocoon harvest of the district is larger for it.

where.text: The location's raw material is Silk

buildings.name: Imperial Relay Station
buildings.text: A post road station maintaining fresh horses and provisions for imperial couriers, enabling messages to travel from the capital to the frontier in days rather than weeks.

buildings.name: Tea Processing House
buildings.text: A workshop where tea leaf is steamed, pounded and pressed into bricks that travel to the frontier markets, where they are exchanged for horses.

buildings.name: Gunpowder Foundry
buildings.text: A military workshop producing fire arrows, incendiary bombs, and proto-rockets from saltpeter, iron, and other materials, the practical application of Tang alchemical discoveries.

buildings.name: Grand Canal Warehouse
buildings.text: A major storage and distribution hub along the Grand Canal, facilitating the flow of grain, silk, and manufactured goods between north and south China.

buildings.name: Confucian Examination Hall
buildings.text: A provincial examination hall where jinshi candidates are tested on literary composition, policy analysis, and moral philosophy, the meritocratic gateway to imperial service.

buildings.name: Border Watchtower
buildings.text: A signal tower on the frontier providing early warning of nomadic incursions through beacon fires visible across vast distances of steppe and desert.

buildings.name: Protectorate Command
buildings.text: The supreme military headquarters for all Tang operations in the western territories, combining garrison command, intelligence gathering, and diplomatic coordination under a single authority.

buildings.name: Imperial Library
buildings.text: The greatest repository of knowledge in human history, housing texts from every civilization and synthesizing them into a unified corpus of learning that advances all fields of human inquiry.

list.name: Sansheng Liubu
list.text: The Three Departments and Six Boards: the Zhongshu (Imperial Secretariat) drafted edicts, the Menxia (Chancellery) reviewed and could veto them, and the Shangshu (Department of State Affairs) executed approved policy through the Six Boards of Personnel, Revenue, Rites, War, Justice, and Works. Inherited and refined from the Sui, the Tang form is the institutional template that every later Chinese dynasty (Song, Yuan, Ming, Qing) adapted. When working, drafted edicts pass review and reach the provinces; when the three departments deadlock, the chancellery vetoes faster than the secretariat can draft, and the boards cease to execute.

list.name: Tang Keju Examinations
list.text: The Tang inherited the Sui examination innovation and elevated the jinshi degree (655) into the prestige path, alongside mingjing (classics), mingfa (law), mingsuan (mathematics), and other tracks. Empress Wu Zetian opened the examinations to a far wider applicant base around 690 and used the resulting jinshi cohorts to break the great-clan grip on senior office. A literate scholar-official class rises on merit; the hereditary aristocracy is permanently barred from the top civilian posts. When the system decays, papers leak, examiners are bribed, and poetry-clique factionalism replaces administrative competence.

list.name: Juntian and Zu-Yong-Diao
list.text: The Equal-Field System (Juntian) granted each adult male a personal-share and inheritance-share of land from imperial reserves; in return he owed Zu (grain), Yong (twenty days' annual labor service), and Diao (a bolt of cloth). Reconstructed from Northern Wei precedent and codified in the Tang Code, the system turned every farmer into a registered taxpayer-soldier. It funded the high Tang from Taizong's reign through the early eighth century. Once powerful clans began absorbing peasant plots, the registers diverged from reality and the 780 Liang Shui Fa replaced it: the same fate awaits any neglected version of the system.

list.name: Fubing Militia System
list.text: From 606 to 749 the Fubing system raised soldiers from the equal-field rolls themselves: each fu garrison rotated men to the capital and the frontier on tours of duty, and soldiers paid their own keep from the land share they held back home. The result was a vast cheap army of motivated landowner-soldiers loyal to the throne. The system's collapse mirrored the equal-field system's: as land registers ran fictitious and rotations went unfilled, the Tang shifted to professional bingmu and to frontier-stationed armies under Jiedushi, whose loyalty to their commander, not the throne, ended the dynasty.

list.name: Yu-shi-tai and the Six Bureaus
list.text: Headed by the yushi dafu, the Tang Censorate organized its work through three divisions (the taiyuan censors at court, the dianyuan staff censors handling daily government, and the chayuan investigating censors auditing officials anywhere in the realm), with the Liushi six bureaus assigning a dedicated watcher to each major board. Censors held the right of direct memorial to the emperor and could impeach any official, including the Grand Councillors. A vigorous Censorate kept officialdom honest; a captured one, with censors bribed by the great clans they were meant to police, accelerated dynastic decline.

list.name: Jiedushi and Frontier Protectorates
list.text: The Anxi Protectorate (640) administered the Tarim Basin and the Western Regions; the Anbei Protectorate (647) governed the steppe nomads; the Anxi-Beiting reorganization extended Tang reach to the Pamirs. From 711 these crystallized into Jiedushi commands: military commissioners holding consolidated military, fiscal, and civilian authority along the frontier. The system gave the high Tang unprecedented strategic depth and supply resilience. It also gave An Lushan, Jiedushi of three frontier commands, the resources to march on Chang'an in 755, the rebellion that broke central Tang power forever.
